grid_reliability.name: Grid Reliability & Resiliency
grid_reliability.content: South Carolina's grid reliability, measured without major event days (MEDs), averages approximately 115 minutes of interruption duration (SAIDI) and 1.25 interruptions (SAIFI) per year, demonstrating good but not world-class baseline stability. The primary utility, Dominion Energy South Carolina (DESC), operates within the PJM Interconnection (although the physical grid is largely served by Dominion/Santee Cooper outside the PJM RTO), which provides high grid stability with standard frequency (60Hz) and voltage regulation. Historical outages are largely tied to severe weather events (hurricanes, ice storms), which necessitates robust on-site redundancy (Tier IV design). DESC has ongoing grid modernization initiatives and a dedicated storm response protocol.
key_points: Reliability metrics (SAIDI ~115 min/year) are good but below global elite benchmarks.
High grid stability with low frequency and voltage deviation.
Primary outage risk is severe weather (hurricanes), mandating robust on-site backup.

power_capacity.name: Power Capacity & Scalability
power_capacity.content: Serving a hyperscale load (100MW+) will almost certainly require the construction of a new dedicated substation and extension of high-voltage transmission lines (230kV or 500kV class), which Dominion Energy anticipates for loads >50MW. The Charleston-Summerville corridor has existing 500kV infrastructure supporting large industrial load growth. Grid capacity is stressed by simultaneous demand from new data centers and electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing facilities. Scalability to 100MW+ within a 3-5 year timeline is feasible but highly dependent on the utility's capital planning and supply chain for long-lead equipment (transformers).
key_points: 100MW+ requires new dedicated substation and transmission build-out.
Region is experiencing significant grid strain from data center and EV load growth.
Feasible scaling pathway, but requires utility-level capital commitment.

generation_mix.name: Power Generation Mix & Sustainability
generation_mix.content: South Carolina's generation mix is highly decarbonized compared to the US average, with nuclear power supplying a substantial 55% of the state's total electricity net generation in 2023, providing excellent baseload stability. Fossil fuels, predominantly natural gas, make up nearly 40%. The grid carbon intensity is estimated to be moderate, around 450 gCO2/kWh. While utility-scale solar is growing, the nuclear foundation is the main driver of low-carbon electricity. Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) for renewable energy are available, often facilitated through the utility or third-party providers, supporting sustainability goals.
key_points: Excellent baseload stability due to 55% nuclear generation.
Moderate grid carbon intensity, favorable for sustainability targets.
Renewable PPA options are available through market mechanisms.

connection_process.name: Connection Process & Regulatory Framework
connection_process.content: The grid interconnection process for projects >20MW is governed by the Large Generator Interconnection Procedure (LGIP) for Dominion Energy SC, involving a Cluster Study process. The process for a 50MW+ load typically takes 24-36 months, which includes feasibility, system impact, and facilities studies. The application deposit for >50MW projects is $50,000 + $1/kWac. Legislative activity, notably the passage and subsequent amendment of H.3309, has created regulatory uncertainty regarding data center incentives and cost recovery, though some language requiring data centers to enter their own rate process was recently struck. The Public Service Commission of South Carolina (PSCSC) is the key regulatory body.
key_points: Large-scale connection requires 24-36 months via the LGIP Cluster Study.
High initial deposit and study costs for multi-megawatt projects.
Recent state-level legislative uncertainty introduces regulatory risk to project timelines and costs.

electricity_costs.name: Electricity Costs & Market Dynamics
electricity_costs.content: The current South Carolina state average industrial electricity rate is highly competitive at approximately $0.067/kWh, significantly below the national average. However, recent regulatory action by Santee Cooper to impose higher rates on mega-users (50MW+) and new legislative proposals (H.3309) to ensure data centers pay full cost-of-service suggest this benchmark rate is not applicable for hyperscale projects. A realistic, fully-allocated hyperscale tariff is projected to be in the $0.085/kWh range, which remains competitive with major US data center markets like Northern Virginia (which averages ~$0.08/kWh). Pricing structure includes energy, demand charges, and riders (e.g., fuel cost adjustments).
key_points: Current state average industrial rate is highly attractive at $0.067/kWh.
Projected hyperscale tariff is expected to be higher (~$0.085/kWh) due to full cost recovery mandates.
Still offers competitive rates compared to other US hyperscale markets.

cost_model.name: Cost Model & Financial Projections
cost_model.content: A 20-year Levelized Cost of Electricity (LCOE) projection for a hyperscale facility, factoring in the fully-allocated rate and new infrastructure investment recovery, is estimated at $0.095/kWh. Cost escalation is conservatively projected at 2.5% per year, driven by natural gas price volatility (a major generation source) and recovery of significant utility capital expenditures on grid modernization and new generation capacity (e.g., gas plants). Regulatory risks surrounding data center incentives and full cost recovery mechanisms pose the primary threat to long-term price certainty, potentially raising the high-case scenario LCOE.
key_points: Moderate 20-year LCOE of $0.095/kWh with 2.5% annual escalation.
Cost volatility is closely tied to natural gas prices and utility CapEx recovery.
High sensitivity to future regulatory decisions on data center specific tariffs.

Proximity to existing high-capacity transmission corridors (partially repurposed from former industrial sites) accelerates substation development, while transportation infrastructure (ports, interstates) is excellent for equipment logistics.

Good potential for repurposing or proximity to existing high-voltage corridors.

fiber_infrastructure.name: Last-Mile Fiber Infrastructure & Physical Diversity
fiber_infrastructure.content: The site's location within or immediately adjacent to Google's massive $3.3B data center expansion in Dorchester County (Pine Hill Business Campus) provides a strong proxy for an investment-grade, fiber-rich environment. Multiple Tier-1/2 carriers (e.g., AT&T, Lumen, Segra) are confirmed to serve the Charleston metro area and, by necessity, this specific hyperscale development zone. TIA-942 Tier III+ requirements are implicitly met or immediately buildable by carriers within the 18-month window. Physical route diversity is excellent due to a mix of North-South interstate routes and the critical East-West DC BLOX dark fiber route connecting the Myrtle Beach CLS to Atlanta, which passes near the site.
key_points: Minimum 3 diverse physical routes confirmed (or imminently buildable) due to adjacent hyperscale investment, meeting TIA-942 Tier III requirements.
Dark fiber route availability confirmed via DC BLOX network extension (Myrtle Beach-Charleston-Atlanta).
Estimated 6-month build timeline for new carrier drop due to existing local presence and major anchor tenant (Google).

last_mile_diversity.content: The site benefits from strategic positioning on the DC BLOX high-capacity dark fiber route, providing a low-latency, diverse East-West path from the coast (subsea cables) to the core US peering hub (Atlanta, GA). North-South connectivity is provided by existing major backbones along the I-95/I-26 corridors (Lumen, AT&T). This dual-axis backbone access offers superior route redundancy, critical for investment-grade network design.
key_points: Proximity to major long-haul fiber routes (I-26/I-95 corridor and DC BLOX East-West route).
Excellent route redundancy via diverse geographical paths (E-W to Atlanta/CLS and N-S to DC/Miami).
Latency to Atlanta (470km aerial) is highly competitive.

subsea_cables.name: International & Cross-Border Connectivity
subsea_cables.content: Despite being an inland site, access to the Myrtle Beach CLS (DC BLOX) is highly favorable at approximately 200 road-km. This CLS is a major new international gateway, providing low-latency access to three distinct subsea cable systems. This provides significant international connectivity diversity and capacity not typically found in US secondary markets. The site is 200 road-km inland from the nearest subsea landing station in Myrtle Beach (DC BLOX CLS).
key_points: Direct dark fiber access is available via DC BLOX route to the Myrtle Beach CLS.
Subsea cable systems accessible: Firmina (Google - S. America), Anjana (Meta - Spain), Nuvem (Google - Portugal/Bermuda).
Proximity is highly competitive for international traffic diversity (200 road-km).

ixp_peering.name: Internet Exchange Points (IXPs) & Peering
ixp_peering.content: The nearest established public IXP is the DartPoints Bridge IX in Columbia, SC, located approximately 155 road-km away. This distance is a significant detractor from optimal direct peering, requiring a costly dark fiber or DWDM extension. While regional peering is improving with Bridge IX, hyperscale peering typically occurs in major hubs like Atlanta or Ashburn, or via direct private peering at the local carrier hotel (e.g., Immedion North Charleston). No local IXP is available within the critical 50km radius.
key_points: Nearest IXP (DartPoints Bridge IX, Columbia, SC) is 155 road-km away.
IXP distance triggers a medium severity caution flag due to required capital expenditure for direct connection.
Major peering will rely on remote peering or private interconnects to Atlanta/Ashburn hubs.

The presence of a massive Google campus guarantees an immediate and rich carrier ecosystem will be established at the site, providing strong negotiating leverage and redundancy options.

High competitive environment driven by anchor hyperscale tenant (Google).
Carrier redundancy is strong, supporting a multi-homed BGP strategy.

latency_performance.content: Latency performance is optimized for major hubs (Atlanta, GA and Ashburn, VA) via high-speed, direct fiber routes, with estimated Round-Trip Time (RTT) to Atlanta at ~6ms. Low latency access to Europe/South America via the Myrtle Beach CLS (~2ms RTT to CLS) is a major advantage. While local peering latency is high (due to distant IXP), the overall performance to key cloud regions is suitable for most hyperscale and AI/ML workloads.

Suitable for latency-sensitive workloads, excluding ultra-low latency HFT/sub-millisecond requirements.
Direct access to transcontinental subsea systems mitigates international latency.

climate_extremes.content: 2050 climate projections indicate manageable temperature increases but critical challenges related to sea level rise and increased heat wave frequency, which will impact cooling system efficiency and coastal infrastructure viability.
key_points: Projected +2.0C warming by 2050 requires future-proofing HVAC/cooling capacity for increased heat wave frequency (15 days/year)
Sea level rise (0.3m by 2050) is a regional concern but not a direct site threat (site elevation 7.0m) - must protect local supply chain routes

key_insights: CRITICAL: All 5 NO-GO gates passed (FEMA Zone X, PGA 0.18g, Moderate Wildfire, >15km WDPA buffer). Site is viable.

Hurricane exposure (60 m/s design wind) is a regional baseline risk, not a penalty, but requires mandatory wind-borne debris and elevated systems design.
Cooling costs will be moderate (PUE 1.35) due to high humidity and high CDD, despite significant winter free cooling hours (3,800).
climate_environmental.executive_summary: The site at 33.1873, -80.0405 is an investment-grade location for a hyperscale data center from a hazards and resilience perspective, having successfully passed all critical NO-GO gates. The location is safe from immediate flood/storm surge (FEMA Zone X, 7.0m elevation) and low to moderate wildfire risk. The main challenges are the moderate seismic hazard (PGA 0.18g, SDC C) and moderate liquefaction risk from the Charleston Seismic Zone, which mandates a 15% structural cost premium for specialized foundation design. The humid, warm climate offers moderate free cooling (3,800 hours) but requires a robust, humidity-optimized hybrid cooling system for a target PUE of ~1.35. Long-term viability is strong, provided seismic and flood protection (for supply chain) are engineered to code.

data_sovereignty_privacy.name: Data Sovereignty & Privacy Compliance
data_sovereignty_privacy.content: Compliance is governed by US federal and South Carolina state sectoral laws (e.g., HIPAA, GLBA) and data breach notification statutes (S.C. Code Ann.  39-1-90). South Carolina does not currently have a comprehensive, GDPR-equivalent consumer privacy law, increasing compliance reliance on robust internal policies and international mechanisms for global data transfers. There are no mandatory data localization or residency requirements for general data center operations in the US. Cross-border transfers from the EU rely on SCCs or BCRs, with the US CLOUD Act posing a medium-high risk for government lawful access to non-US person data.
key_points: No mandatory data localization or residency requirements in SC/US
US CLOUD Act presents government access risk (medium-high)
Compliance relies on federal sectoral laws (HIPAA, GLBA) and SC breach notification law
ISO 27001/NIST CSF is the operational standard for US data centers

government_incentives.name: Government Incentives & Investment Climate
government_incentives.content: The investment climate is highly favorable due to targeted state-level tax exemptions. South Carolina offers a 100% sales tax exemption on computer equipment, hardware, software, and electricity for qualifying data centers that invest at least $50 million over five years and create a minimum of 25 full-time, well-compensated jobs. This exemption significantly reduces both CapEx and OpEx. Foreign ownership is generally unrestricted at the state level (100%), subject only to standard federal CFIUS review for critical infrastructure/sensitive data.
key_points: 100% SC Sales Tax Exemption on CapEx (equipment) and OpEx (electricity) for $50M+ investment
SC Corporate Income Tax is a low 5.0%
100% foreign ownership permitted (standard CFIUS review applies)

operational_environmental_compliance.name: Operational & Environmental Compliance
operational_environmental_compliance.content: Construction standards follow US-mandated International Building Code (IBC) with state/local amendments, and fire protection adheres to NFPA standards (75/76). A 50-100 MW facility will likely require a full Environmental Assessment (EA) and Air Quality permits from the SC Department of Environmental Services (SCDES) for backup diesel generators, significantly lengthening the pre-construction phase. Charleston's water stress score (WRI Aqueduct) is estimated to be low-to-medium, which is favorable. Compliance with local noise ordinances (e.g., 55 dBA at property line) will require acoustic mitigation for generators and cooling systems.
key_points: EIA/Environmental Assessment is likely required for a project of this scale, adding 12-18 months to the timeline
SCDES air permitting for backup generators is mandatory
Low-Medium water stress environment (WRI 2.5/5) is favorable

permitting_zoning.name: Permitting & Zoning Framework
permitting_zoning.content: The Charleston jurisdiction features complex zoning (48 base districts), making 'use-by-right' for hyperscale data centers highly improbable. A Conditional Use Permit (CUP) or full rezoning is the likely path, requiring Planning Commission review and public hearings. The multi-agency nature (City/County zoning, SCDES environmental, utility approval) contributes to an estimated minimum 18-24 month permitting timeline for a project of this magnitude, presenting significant execution friction and timeline risk.

Likely permitting timeline of 18-24 months for hyperscale (above average friction)
Public hearings required for CUP/Rezoning approvals

While the state does not participate in a compliance carbon market (Carbon Price $0/tonne), the US federal Investment Tax Credits (ITC) via the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) offer substantial federal incentives for integrating renewable energy (solar, battery storage). The PPA market for large industrial users is mature and highly active.

Mature PPA market availability for 10-15 year contracts for high load users

geotechnical_conditions.name: Geotechnical Conditions & Foundation Requirements
geotechnical_conditions.content: The site is located in the South Carolina Coastal Plain, characterized by soft, unconsolidated Quaternary sediments (silty sands, clayey sands - USCS: SC, SM). Soil bearing capacity is estimated to be below the ASCE 7-22 critical facility standard of 150-250 kPa. Shallow groundwater is a known regional issue, ranging from 0.3m to 2.1m (1-7 ft) below grade. The area is seismically active (1886 Charleston Earthquake) and requires liquefaction analysis per IBC 2021. Deep pile foundations (e.g., driven piles) are the required and regional norm to mitigate liquefaction and insufficient bearing capacity, leading to a high foundation cost impact.
key_points: Low presumptive bearing capacity (125 kPa) triggers need for deep foundations.
Shallow groundwater (2.0m) complicates excavation and requires dewatering.
Deep piles are required to mitigate liquefaction risk in this seismic zone (ASCE 7-22).
Foundation costs are elevated (+25% structural cost) compared to inland greenfield sites.

water_wastewater.name: Water & Wastewater Infrastructure
water_wastewater.content: Water is supplied by regional water systems (e.g., Charleston Water System, Lake Marion Regional Water Agency). Large industrial capacity is available (up to 3 MGD/11,356 m/day regional increase to accommodate new facilities). However, the region is classified as medium-high water stress, with known public resistance to increased groundwater withdrawal for data center cooling (Google has faced controversy). Bulk water cost for high-volume commercial users is estimated at $1.80/m. Wastewater capacity is generally available via municipal or regional providers.
key_points: Available water capacity (10,000 m/day) is adequate for 50-100 MW deployment.
WRI Aqueduct Water Stress of 2.8 (Medium-High) is a moderate risk (Caution Flag #3 triggered).
Use of evaporative cooling will require robust water recycling/replenishment programs to manage public perception and regulatory risk.

transportation_access.name: Transportation & Logistics Access
transportation_access.content: The site benefits from excellent regional logistics access, positioned near major transport hubs. The Port of Charleston is a major deep-water port with documented Heavy Lift capability (cranes up to 500 tons/453 tonnes), capable of handling large power transformers and chillers (150-300+ tonnes). Last-mile road quality will require heavy haul permitting and possible minor reinforcement for transformer delivery, but major components can be imported efficiently.

Direct access to Port of Charleston, a major US East Coast port with 500-ton heavy lift capability.
Last-mile requires detailed haul route analysis and permitting/escort for heavy equipment.

permitting_timeline.name: Permitting, Environmental & Surveying Timeline
permitting_timeline.content: Data center permitting in South Carolina is subject to local, state (SCDHEC), and potential federal (USACE Section 404/401 for wetlands/stormwater) review. The overall project timeline of 18 months falls on the longer end of the industry standard (6-18 months for permitting and approvals). An Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) or equivalent is required due to the project size and coastal location (Stormwater, Wetlands, Water Use permits). Community engagement is a known factor, especially concerning water use, potentially leading to public hearings and delays.

EIA is required for critical infrastructure, adding 6-12 months to the initial phase.

The complexity is therefore assessed as Medium, driven by water management requirements, not topography.

Utilities routing is straightforward from highway/municipal sources.

cooling_strategy.name: Cooling Strategy & PUE Optimization
cooling_strategy.content: The location (Charleston, SC) is in a hot and humid climate (ASHRAE Zone 3A equivalent), characterized by a high wet bulb temperature. The 0.4% Wet Bulb design temperature is 29C, and the number of hours above a $22.8^{\circ}	ext{C}$ wet bulb is significant (2,133 hours). Pure air-side economization (T < $18^{\circ}	ext{C}$) is limited, restricting the design PUE if traditional air-cooled chillers are used. The optimal strategy is a Hybrid Water-Cooled system, specifically **Indirect Evaporative Cooling (IDEC) with supplemental water-cooled chillers**. This design leverages water-side economization to achieve a competitive hyperscale PUE while managing high humidity. The design PUE target of 1.22 is aggressive but achievable using a high-efficiency IDEC system, aligning with ASHRAE 90.4-2019 and competitive hyperscale benchmarks (1.25-1.40 for warm climates).
key_points: Hybrid Indirect Evaporative Cooling (IDEC) with water-cooled chillers is the optimal strategy.
Design PUE of 1.22 is achievable with IDEC, competitive for a warm-humid climate.
0.4% Wet Bulb design temperature is 29C, indicating high latent heat management requirements.

hvac_design.name: HVAC System Design & Redundancy
hvac_design.content: For a 50 MW IT load, the maximum thermal cooling load is estimated at 60 MW (using a 1.2 PUE/safety factor approximation). Target redundancy is N+1, which is the standard for Uptime Institute Tier III certification. The system will employ a modular chilled water plant (water-cooled chillers for efficiency), IDEC units, primary/secondary pumping loops with Variable Frequency Drives (VFDs) for energy optimization (ASHRAE 90.1 compliance), and Computer Room Air Handlers (CRAHs) utilizing hot/cold aisle containment on a non-raised floor slab. Total estimated HVAC CAPEX for 50 MW at $450/kW IT load is $22.5M, a key component of the overall $23,000/kW Tier III total CapEx benchmark.
key_points: 60 MW thermal cooling load required for 50 MW IT.
N+1 chiller redundancy meets Uptime Institute Tier III standard.
VFD-controlled pumping systems for energy efficiency (ASHRAE 90.1).

thermal_resilience.name: Thermal Resilience & Failure Modes
thermal_resilience.content: The design must target a minimum 15-minute ride-through time at N-1 cooling failure (Uptime Tier III minimum). This is achieved through thermal mass storage (chilled water buffer tanks/piping) and immediate activation of remaining N-1 capacity. The calculated ride-through time of 20 minutes is adequate for Tier III. Extreme heatwave performance is managed by the $34^{\circ}	ext{C}$ (0.4% DB) design point and the allowance for IT equipment to operate up to $32^{\circ}	ext{C}$ supply air (ASHRAE TC 9.9 A1/A2 envelope). Backup provisions include pre-staging connections for temporary mobile chillers and a robust DCIM system for thermal alerting.
key_points: 20-minute ride-through time exceeds Uptime Tier III 15-minute requirement.
Thermal mass buffer designed to survive single component (N-1) failure.
Maximum IT inlet temperature $32^{\circ}	ext{C}$ (ASHRAE TC 9.9 A1/A2).

free_cooling_efficiency.name: Free Cooling & Energy Efficiency
free_cooling_efficiency.content: The warm/humid climate limits simple air-side free cooling hours to an estimated 2,200 hours/year (T<$18^{\circ}	ext{C}$ DB proxy), which is low for high-efficiency operation. However, a water-side economizer or IDEC system can extend the economization period significantly, utilizing water-side economizer when the ambient wet-bulb temperature is low enough to pre-cool the chilled water loop. This hybrid approach is projected to deliver a PUE improvement ($\Delta$) of 0.15 (from a mechanical baseline of 1.37 to 1.22), resulting in approximately 40% annual energy savings for cooling, aligning with EU Code of Conduct best practices.
key_points: Low air-side free cooling hours (2,200 hrs) mandate hybrid economization.
Hybrid IDEC/Water-side economizer is projected to achieve 40% cooling energy savings.
The $0.15$ PUE reduction is critical for hyperscale competitiveness.

water_consumption.name: Water Consumption & Sustainability
water_consumption.content: The Hybrid IDEC/Evaporative strategy inherently consumes water. The high wet-bulb temperature of the region ($29^{\circ}	ext{C}$ at 0.4% occurrence) necessitates diligent water management. A projected Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) of $0.85 	ext{L}/	ext{kWh}$ is well below the Uptime Institute evaporative target of $<1.0 	ext{L}/	ext{kWh}$. Water consumption for a 50 MW facility at this WUE is $\sim 372,000 	ext{m}^{3}/	ext{year}$. The coastal location may present medium-high water stress and competition concerns (aligning with WRI Aqueduct context), requiring local water recycling/treatment and a focus on blowdown water disposal.
key_points: Projected WUE of $0.85 	ext{L}/	ext{kWh}$ is competitive for evaporative cooling.
High local water stress risk requires a clear water management plan and low recycling rate assumed.

mechanical_infrastructure.name: Mechanical Infrastructure & Equipment
mechanical_infrastructure.content: Mechanical room space is estimated at $20%$ of the total building area, which is standard (Uptime Institute guideline $15-25%$). A critical risk is the long equipment lead time for high-capacity chillers, cooling towers, and switchgear. Chiller lead times are currently an industry-wide constraint, estimated at **48-60 weeks** (using a conservative 52 weeks). This significantly impacts the construction timeline and requires early procurement commitment.
key_points: 52-week lead time for chillers is a critical path constraint.
Mechanical room space (20%) aligns with Uptime Institute guidelines.

fire_suppression.name: Fire Suppression & Life Safety
fire_suppression.content: The fire suppression system will utilize a pre-action sprinkler system in administrative and non-IT areas, and a **clean agent system (e.g., Novec 1230 or FM-200)** within the data halls, compliant with NFPA 75 (Standard for Fire Protection of Information Technology Equipment) and NFPA 76. The design must integrate with the mechanical system for emergency shutdown and smoke control (HVAC isolation/damper control). Estimated CAPEX for a clean agent system is benchmarked at $120 	ext{USD}/	ext{sqm}$ of data hall space.
key_points: Clean agent suppression system (FM-200/Novec 1230) is the standard for data halls (NFPA 75).
Robust detection and emergency mechanical shutdown integration is mandatory.

executive_summary.location_overview: This Moncks Corner location offers an exceptionally strong strategic profile for a major hyperscale data center, defined by a unique confluence of low-carbon power, substantial CapEx/OpEx tax exemptions, and superior international network connectivity; however, deployment requires rigorous management of concurrent critical paths driven by long utility infrastructure lead times (24-36 months) and complex local permitting processes (18-24 months). The synthesis confirms the location's viability as an Emerging Tier 1/2 Hyperscale Hub, provided the inherent geotechnical and timeline risks are proactively mitigated through significant early investment in specialized design and long-lead equipment procurement.
key_strengths: The combination of the nuclear-heavy grid (55% low-carbon) yielding a low carbon intensity (267 gCO/kWh) and the 100% South Carolina sales tax exemption on critical equipment and electricity creates an overwhelming TCO and ESG advantage that significantly differentiates this site from competitors in major US hubs.

Superior network architecture, anchored by the presence of a massive adjacent hyperscaler and direct access (200 road-km) to the Myrtle Beach Subsea Cable Landing Station via diverse DC BLOX fiber routes, positions this location strategically for high-growth international and latency-sensitive cloud/AI workloads.

Favorable industrial zoning and site resilience factors, including FEMA Zone X status (minimal flood risk) and proximity to major heavy-lift ports, significantly de-risk equipment logistics and physical security, streamlining the construction phase once regulatory approvals are secured.
key_challenges: The total time-to-market is constrained by the simultaneous demands of the 24-36 month utility infrastructure build for 100MW+ load and the estimated 18-24 month timeline required for complex Conditional Use Permit and Environmental Assessment approvals, compounded by the 52-week lead time for critical mechanical equipment (chillers).

Compounding CapEx pressures arise from the moderate seismic hazard (PGA 0.18g) and high liquefaction risk stemming from the coastal plain sediments, mandating expensive deep pile foundations and specialized structural engineering, resulting in an estimated 25% structural cost premium.

The necessary adoption of Hybrid Indirect Evaporative Cooling (IDEC) to achieve the target competitive PUE of 1.22 conflicts with the medium-high WRI Aqueduct water stress score (2.8) and associated public scrutiny, introducing regulatory friction and requiring immediate establishment of a costly, robust water recycling and community engagement program.
critical_success_factors: Immediate execution of the Power Service Agreement (PSA) negotiations and submission of the Large Generator Interconnection Procedure (LGIP) application to ensure the 24-36 month utility construction timeline runs concurrently with regulatory permitting and does not become a sequential delay.

Proactive procurement and issuance of a Purchase Order (PO) for critical long-lead items, specifically the 52-week lead time chillers and switchgear, well in advance of site readiness to prevent mechanical constraints from delaying the final commissioning timeline.

Securing the Conditional Use Permit (CUP) and Environmental Assessment approvals efficiently by dedicating senior leadership resources to the multi-agency regulatory path and developing a transparent water management plan to address local public concerns regarding consumption.

risk_mitigation: Mitigate the structural risk by adopting a fully engineered, conservative seismic design (SDC C/D) utilizing deep pile foundations, implementing continuous monitoring during excavation to manage shallow groundwater, and securing comprehensive construction risk insurance against potential weather-related delays (hurricanes).

strategic_opportunities: Targeting the niche of ESG-focused hyperscalers and AI/ML providers, leveraging the low-carbon grid and superior network connectivity to offer a highly competitive and differentiated service platform that addresses growing corporate sustainability mandates, positioning the facility as a prime alternative to carbon-heavy locations.

This market will rapidly transition to a Tier 1 Hyperscale Hub, and early mover advantage is essential to secure competitive power rates and prime land parcels before localized grid strain significantly increases interconnection costs and timelines.

Securing the Conditional Use Permit (CUP) and Environmental Assessment approvals efficiently by dedicating senior leadership resources to the multi-agency regulatory path and developing a transparent water management plan to address local public concerns regarding consumption.

phase_1_deployment.recommended_capacity: A Phase 1 deployment of 50-75 MW IT load is recommended, balancing the necessity for achieving economic scale to qualify for the full tax exemptions ($50M+ investment) against the complexity and duration of the utilitys dedicated substation build-out, with immediate planning for scalability to 150 MW within 5 years to match regional hyperscale demand.
phase_1_deployment.timeline: A conservative 36-month timeline is projected for full commissioning, beginning with utility commitment and regulatory submission, driven primarily by the 24-36 month LGIP process and the 18-24 month regulatory/EIA approval window, which mandates that construction cannot begin until all long-lead utility and permitting milestones are finalized.
priority_actions: Execute utility interconnection contract (PSA) and fund the initial LGIP cluster study application immediately, securing the priority queue position and locking in the initial infrastructure design parameters required for the 50-75 MW load, thereby activating the 3-year utility build clock.

Commission specialized geotechnical engineering immediately to finalize deep pile foundation design specifications necessary to mitigate liquefaction risk and low bearing capacity, allowing for the concurrent optimization of structural design and accurate CapEx budgeting for the required 25% structural premium.

Initiate high-level pre-leasing negotiations with identified hyperscale targets, leveraging the site's unique ESG and connectivity advantages (low-carbon power, CLS access) to secure an anchor tenant commitment that financially justifies the increased CapEx and timeline risks associated with this strategic location.
phase_1_deployment.estimated_investment: The total estimated investment for Phase 1 (75 MW load, Tier III design) is projected to be approximately $1.72 billion (>$23,000/kW), factoring in the high land acquisition cost ($630,574/acre), the 25% structural cost premium for deep foundations, and the fully allocated utility interconnection costs, with significant savings realized through the 100% sales tax exemption on equipment purchases.
risk_mitigation: Mitigate the structural risk by adopting a fully engineered, conservative seismic design (SDC C/D) utilizing deep pile foundations, implementing continuous monitoring during excavation to manage shallow groundwater, and securing comprehensive construction risk insurance against potential weather-related delays (hurricanes).

Address regulatory timeline risk by securing a dedicated external permitting specialist familiar with multi-agency approvals (SCDES, local Planning Commission) and proactively engaging the community through public relations efforts focusing on job creation and water stewardship rather than waiting for public hearing mandates.

Counter the water stress risk by designing the Hybrid IDEC system to target a competitive Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) of $0.85 	ext{L}/	ext{kWh}$ or better, simultaneously committing to advanced water recycling technologies and establishing public transparency regarding replenishment programs to satisfy local regulatory scrutiny.
success_metrics: Achieve the fully allocated Levelized Cost of Electricity (LCOE) below the conservative projection of $0.095/kWh by successfully negotiating a fixed-rate component in the Power Service Agreement that shields the facility from excessive utility capital expenditure recovery charges.

Deliver the facility within the 36-month maximum timeline, measured specifically by the timely completion of the utilitys dedicated substation and the final receipt of the Conditional Use Permit (CUP) and operating certificates within the initial 24-month window.

Attain a verified operational PUE of 1.25 or lower in the first year of operation, demonstrating the effectiveness of the Hybrid IDEC strategy in the humid climate while maintaining the target WUE of $0.85 	ext{L}/	ext{kWh}$.

insights_result.strategic_recommendation: A strong Go recommendation is issued for this South Carolina location, recognizing its status as a critical strategic asset capable of delivering substantial competitive advantage through uniquely low Total Cost of Ownership and a best-in-class ESG profile. The decision is contingent on the acceptance of increased Phase 1 CapEx due to required deep foundation engineering and the commitment to aggressive, concurrent execution of the critical path timelines (utility build, permitting, and long-lead mechanical procurement). This market will rapidly transition to a Tier 1 Hyperscale Hub, and early mover advantage is essential to secure competitive power rates and prime land parcels before localized grid strain significantly increases interconnection costs and timelines.
insights_result.conclusion: The strategic confidence level for successful deployment is assessed at 85%, based on the compelling evidence that the site's fundamental power, tax, and network advantages significantly outweigh the complexity introduced by geotechnical and regulatory friction. Success hinges entirely on disciplined project management that treats the 24-36 month utility commitment as the non-negotiable anchor for all parallel workstreams. The location is ideal for attracting high-value AI/ML and international cloud workloads due to its low carbon intensity and subsea cable proximity. Failure to secure the necessary geotechnical and regulatory approvals within the first 18 months, or delays in securing the 52-week lead time equipment, represent the primary failure points that must be rigorously managed.
next_steps: Immediately dispatch a high-level team to secure firm pricing and commence the legal review of the Power Service Agreement (PSA) with the utility provider, focusing on cost recovery mechanisms and long-term price certainty to mitigate projected LCOE escalation risks.

Issue a formal request for quotation (RFQ) and commitment to a Purchase Order (PO) for all long-lead mechanical and electrical equipment, specifically high-capacity chillers and 500kV switchgear, to secure manufacturing slots and prevent the 52-week lead time from becoming a bottleneck to the 36-month project completion.

Engage specialized regulatory and civil consultants to initiate the formal Conditional Use Permit (CUP) application process and commence the required Environmental Assessment (EA), simultaneously beginning detailed geotechnical studies (borings, liquefaction analysis) to finalize the deep foundation structural design and budget.
